body:
Short answer: What is uplighting? It is event lighting where small fixtures sit on the floor and shine colored light up walls, columns, drapery or trees. It is the fastest way to change the mood of a space, and a typical layout uses about one uplight every 6 to 10 feet of wall, set to a single color or programmed to change through the night.

[[IMAGE]]

This guide covers what uplighting is, where uplights go, wired vs battery fixtures, color choices, how many uplights you need, how uplighting compares with other event lighting, and what to check with your venue.

What is uplighting?

An uplight is a compact fixture placed on the floor, close to a surface, and aimed upward. The beam spreads up the surface and fades as it rises, which gives that familiar glow on walls at weddings, galas and corporate events.

Uplighting does not light your guests. It lights the architecture around them. That is why it works so well: the space feels finished and colored, while people still look natural under the general light.

Most event uplights today are LED, which means they run cool, draw little power and can mix almost any color from red, green, blue and often white or amber diodes.

Where uplights go

  • Walls — The most common placement. Space fixtures evenly along the perimeter, about 6 to 18 inches from the wall, so each beam overlaps the next.
  • Columns and pillars — One fixture at the base of each column makes the structure stand out. Wide columns may need two, one on each face.
  • Drapery and pipe-and-drape — Fabric takes color beautifully. Uplighting a white or ivory drape is a quick way to turn a plain backdrop into a feature wall.
  • Trees and plants — Indoor trees, floral arches and outdoor trees look great lit from below. Outdoors, use fixtures rated for the weather.
  • Bars, stages and entrances — A few uplights on a bar front, stage skirt or entry arch guide guests and add depth to photos.

Wired vs battery (wireless) uplights

Both types give the same look on the wall. The difference is how they get power and how they are controlled.

  • Wired uplights — Plug into wall power and often link together with data cable. They run for as long as the event lasts, but you need outlets near the fixtures and a safe, taped or covered cable path.
  • Battery uplights — Run on internal batteries and are usually controlled wirelessly. They set up fast, leave no cables on the floor and suit historic venues or spaces with few outlets. Check the runtime at the brightness you plan to use, and charge them fully before load-in.

Many events mix the two: battery fixtures in the middle of the floor or along glass walls, wired fixtures where power is easy.

Choosing colors, including brand colors

Color is the main decision in uplighting. A few practical points:

  • Warm amber or soft white — Flatters skin and wood, and works for dinners and formal events.
  • Blues and purples — Read as evening and party. They are popular for dancing but can make a space feel darker.
  • Brand colors — Send hex or Pantone values early. LED fixtures mix most colors closely, but deep oranges, browns and some pastels are hard to match exactly.
  • Test on the real surface — Beige paint, brick and wood all shift color. What looks right on a white wall can turn muddy on a warm one.

How many uplights do I need?

A typical rule of thumb is one uplight every 6 to 10 feet of wall you want to light. Six feet gives a continuous wash with no dark gaps. Ten feet gives a scalloped pattern of distinct pools, which many people prefer.

To estimate, measure the length of the walls you plan to light (not always the full perimeter, since doors, windows and service areas are often skipped), divide by 6 and by 10 for a range, then add one or two fixtures per column or feature.

Space (typical)Wall to lightUplights at 10 ftUplights at 6 ft
Small private event spaceabout 80 ft813 to 14
Mid-size ballroom or loftabout 200 ft2033 to 34
Large ballroom or hallabout 300 ft3050
Tent, 40 x 60 ftabout 200 ft perimeter2033 to 34, plus poles

These are starting points. Tall walls, dark finishes and bright house lights all call for tighter spacing. Low ceilings and pale walls let you spread out.

Uplighting vs pin spots vs gobos vs stage wash

Uplighting is one layer of event lighting. Most well-lit events combine several.

TypeWhat it lightsBest for
UplightingWalls, columns, drape, treesOverall color and mood
Pin spotsCenterpieces, cakes, displaysMaking tables and details pop
Gobo / monogramA pattern or logo on a wall or floorNames, logos, textures
Stage washSpeakers and performersMaking people visible and on camera

If you have a stage, uplighting is not enough on its own. Presenters need front light, and that usually means a wash on a truss or stands. Our stage rental in NYC covers decks, truss and the lighting that goes on them.

Lighting for camera and livestream

Uplighting looks great in photos and video, but cameras see it differently than people do.

  • Light faces separately — Keep a neutral key light on speakers. Saturated color on faces looks wrong on camera.
  • Set white balance for the stage — Not for the wall color, or skin tones will shift.
  • Watch brightness — Very bright uplights behind a speaker can overpower the camera exposure. Dim the wall behind the lectern a little.
  • Avoid flicker — Use fixtures and dimming settings that do not flicker at camera frame rates.

For more on cameras and streaming at events, see our hybrid event AV and streaming guide.

Venue rules: power, cables and the fire marshal

Check these with your venue before you plan the layout:

  • Power — Where outlets are, which circuits are free, and whether the venue has its own lighting rules or in-house vendors.
  • Cable paths — Most venues want cables taped down, covered with ramps, or run along walls. Battery fixtures avoid most of this.
  • Fire code — Exits, exit signs and egress paths must stay clear and visible. Drapery usually needs a flame-retardant certificate, and some New York venues ask for paperwork before load-in.
  • Load-in time — Uplighting is quick to place, but programming colors and checking each fixture takes time. Ask for enough access before doors.

Uplighting for events: static color or changing looks

The simplest setup is one static color for the whole night. It is reliable and often all you need.

The step up is DMX control from a lighting desk. Fixtures are addressed and grouped, and looks are built in advance: soft amber for dinner, a brighter tone for speeches, deeper color and slow movement for dancing. An operator triggers each look on cue, so the lighting follows the run of show instead of staying fixed.

Possible AV builds its lighting around Aputure fixtures and provides a lighting desk and operator, so changing looks are part of the plan from the start. If your event calls for a specific type of uplight, we source it.

Uplighting rental: what to ask for

When you request uplighting rental, include the venue, wall lengths or a floor plan, number of columns, colors or brand values, whether you want static color or changing looks, and whether there will be a stage, speakers or a livestream. With that, a quote can include the right number of fixtures, power plan and crew. See our lighting services for the full kit.

Frequently asked questions

What is uplighting?

Uplighting is event lighting where small fixtures sit on the floor and shine color up a wall, column, drape or tree. It changes the color and mood of a space without lighting the guests directly.

How many uplights do I need?

A common rule of thumb is one uplight every 6 to 10 feet of wall you want to light. Measure the walls you plan to cover, divide by 6 for a full wash or by 10 for a lighter look, then add one or two per column.

Are battery uplights better than wired uplights?

Battery uplights remove cable runs and set up faster, which helps in venues with few outlets or strict cable rules. Wired uplights run as long as you need and suit long events, but every fixture needs power and a safe cable path.

Can uplights match our brand colors?

Yes. RGB-type fixtures can mix close to most brand colors. Send your hex or Pantone values ahead and test them on the actual wall surface, since paint, wood and fabric all shift how a color reads.

Does uplighting look good on camera?

It can, as long as the people on camera have their own key light. Saturated uplighting on walls makes a nice background, but it should not be the light on faces, and the camera's white balance should be set for the stage light, not the wall color.

Do I need a lighting operator for uplighting?

Not for a single static color. If you want looks that change through the night, such as dinner, speeches and dancing, a lighting desk and an operator make the changes on cue.
